hook: Follow a single river from a mountain to the sea. It starts cold, fast and full of oxygen, slows and warms as it crosses farmland, mixes with seawater in a muddy, food-rich estuary, and finally reaches an ocean so deep that most of it never sees sunlight. Each stretch is a different aquatic biome, set by salt, light, depth and oxygen.

prereq.q: Which is an abiotic factor of a lake?
prereq.why: Temperature is nonliving; the others are living.

prereq.q: Which two factors mostly decide terrestrial biomes?
prereq.why: Climate (temperature and precipitation) sets land biomes.

figure.caption: The zones of a lake, set by depth and light.

chain.effect: plants and algae grow only in the sunlit photic zone

chain.cause: Rivers carry nutrients to coasts and estuaries
chain.effect: shallow, sunlit coastal water is very productive

chain.cause: Warm or still water holds less dissolved oxygen
chain.effect: fish and other animals there have less oxygen to use

ideas: Aquatic biomes are sorted by salinity, depth, light, temperature and dissolved oxygen: the freshwater biome (lakes, rivers, wetlands) and marine biomes (estuary, intertidal zone, coral reef, open ocean).
A lake has a littoral zone (shallow edge), limnetic zone (open sunlit water), profundal zone (deep, dark) and benthic zone (bottom).
Only the photic zone has enough light for photosynthesis; below it is the aphotic zone.
Estuaries, salt marshes and mangrove forests grow more life per square meter than almost anywhere on Earth: nutrients plus light plus shelter.

misconception.wrong: The open ocean grows the most life per square meter because it is so large.
misconception.right: The open ocean grows a lot in total because it is huge, but each square meter grows little: nutrients are scarce in the sunlit surface. Coral reefs, estuaries and wetlands grow far more per square meter.

summary: Aquatic biomes differ mainly in salinity, depth, light, temperature and dissolved oxygen. Freshwater biomes include lakes (with littoral, limnetic, profundal and benthic zones), rivers and wetlands; marine biomes include estuaries, the intertidal zone, coral reefs and the open ocean. Plants and algae need the photic zone, and colder, moving water holds more oxygen.
